_readme: Every number in here is a tuning knob. Change a value, reload the page, done - no code changes.
Temperatures are in degrees Celsius. Ambient (air) temperature starts at 20 and is set by the slider.
group         which heading the button appears under in the side panel
category      static = never moves | powder = falls and piles | liquid = falls and spreads | gas = rises
density       heavier sinks through lighter. This is what makes sand sink, ice float and oil sit on water.
fallSpeed     max cells moved per frame (rise speed for gases)
slide         powders only: chance of sliding diagonally. 0.9 = loose (dry sand), 0.1 = sluggish (wet mud)
repose        powders only: how far the ground beside it has to fall away before it will slip.
1 = collapses into a flat cone (dry sand), 5 = holds a steep heap (wet mud).
This is the angle of repose, and it is what makes wet ground look different from dry.
spread        liquids only: how far sideways it will look for somewhere to fall from
flowSteps     liquids only: how many sideways moves it gets per frame. This is the main dial for how
quickly a poured puddle settles down flat. Water 4, oil 3, lava 1 (it barely creeps).
moveChance    chance it shifts about of its own accord this frame - creeping, sliding, settling.
Lower = thick and sticky (lava, wet mud). Falling is not covered by it: gravity is
not a matter of choice, so everything drops at its own fallSpeed whatever this says.
drift         gases only: chance of wandering sideways
conductivity  how fast this material takes on its neighbours' temperature (0 = perfect insulator)
cooling       how fast it drifts back to the air temperature on its own, as a fraction of the gap
coolsBy       degrees given up per frame on its own account, whatever the air is doing, stopping
at the air temperature. This is how something that starts white hot cools: at its
own pace rather than twice as fast because the weather turned, and evenly through
the whole of it, so a lava flow stiffens all at once instead of from the edges in.
defaultTemp   the temperature it is created at
emit          a heat source holds itself at this temperature (fire, lava). Water can overwhelm it.
emitRate      how strongly it holds that temperature. Lower = easier to quench.
radiates      degrees per frame thrown at all eight neighbours, on top of what conduction carries.
This is how fire spreads sideways: a flame rises off whatever lit it far too fast to
warm its neighbours by touch, so without this a pool of oil would sit under a fire
and never light, and a row of plants would only ever burn from below. Nothing is
heated past the temperature of whatever is heating it.
clings        chance per frame that a flame stays put instead of rising, while there is something
flammable beside it. Fire is a gas, so without this it leaves the moment it appears
and never stays next to anything long enough to light it.
glowTemp      the temperature the colour fade treats as fully hot, where color is the hot end and
color2 the cold one. A heat source glows up to its own emit, which is the default.
Something that only glows on its way down - cooling scoria - names it here instead.
forceTemp     drags its cell to this temperature in BOTH directions - used by the two ray tools,
which is how the cold ray can chill things rather than only heat them
forceRate     how hard it drags
meltPoint     above this temperature it turns into meltsInto
freezePoint   below this temperature it turns into freezesInto
freezeNeedsGround  it has to have landed on something before it will set solid. Scoria uses this,
so a sinking lump keeps sinking instead of turning to stone in mid water and
leaving a slab of it hanging with nothing underneath.
insulatedBy   what counts as being buried - list the material itself as well, since lava under
more lava is just as covered up as lava under a crust - and insulatedCooling is
how much of its own cooling is left while it is. It is the cell directly above
that decides, which is all being buried amounts to one cell at a time.
In short:
own cooling is left while one is lying on it. Buried scoria gives up heat a tenth
as fast as bare scoria, and buried lava a tenth as fast again - a hundredth of the
open rate - so a flow that has crusted over stays molten underneath for a long
time, and only what is actually exposed to the sky sets at any speed.
bedrockKeepsMolten  resting on the very bottom row of the world, it never sets by cooling alone -
the floor of the world is the heat the world sits on. Water can still put it out.
boilPoint     above this temperature it turns into boilsInto and puffs out boilEmits
depositPoint  a gas condensing where the AIR is below this turns straight into depositsInto,
a solid, instead of into a liquid. This is steam falling as snow rather than rain.
contacts      what it turns into depending on what it comes to rest ON: snow melting the
moment it lands in water, or packing down into ice where it settles on ice
windLift      how readily the wind tool picks it up, 0 to 1. Leave it out and it follows from
the category: gases 1, powders 0.5, liquids 0.1, anything fixed 0.
tool          marks an entry as a tool rather than a material. The wind tool is not placed
into the world; dragging it blows things about and stirs up the air.
ignitePoint   above this temperature it catches fire: becomes burnsInto for burnLife frames, leaving emberInto
quenchedInto  what it becomes the moment it touches water (the water flashes to steam)
wetsInto      what it becomes when water soaks into it. Sand -> Wet Sand -> Wet Mud.
latent        how much heat it has to soak up past the threshold before the change actually happens.
This is why ice sits in a puddle for a few seconds instead of vanishing, but melts
almost instantly against a flame. 0 means the change is immediate.
blastRadius   how far the explosion reaches. Anything explosive lights a fuse instead of burning.
fuse          frames between being lit and going off
blastProof    survives explosions (only the wall does)
growHeight    the tallest a plant can grow, in cells. growHeightMin is the shortest; each plant
picks a height somewhere between the two, so a row of them is not all one size.
growChance    chance per frame of putting on another cell of growth
flowerInto    what the growing tip opens into when it is fully grown. Leave it out and the plant
simply stops - which is what grass on wet sand does.
seedChance    chance per frame that a flower drops a seed
seedWaterRange  how close water has to be before it will set seed at all - this far to the sides
and above, and four times as far below, since the flower is up on a stem while the
water it lives on is down at the roots. A plant somewhere dry lives out its life
but never reproduces.
sprouts       what a seed can come up on and what it becomes there. Wet mud gives a full plant,
wet sand gives short grass with no flower. Dry ground gives nothing at all.
submergedInto is what it comes up as instead when the ground it landed on is at
the bottom of open water - that is how a lily starts. The choice is made on the
single frame the seed germinates and is never looked at again, so draining the
pond afterwards leaves the lily growing.
submergedDepth  how deep the water standing over a seed has to be before it counts as being
underwater rather than in a puddle
sproutMinTemp the seed will not germinate below this temperature
growStyle     how a plant puts on growth. Left out, it climbs as an ordinary stem. "netting"
weaves up through water as an open mesh; "surface" creeps sideways along the
top of the water as a lily pad does.
floatChance   chance that a new one of these is buoyant. This is settled the moment the
particle is created and never revisited, so a seed that came up a floater stays
one. A buoyant one weighs floatDensity instead of its own density, which is what
makes it rise to the surface, ride on it and wander to one side, while the rest
of them sink straight to the bottom.
floatDensity  the weight a buoyant one has. Put it below water's density to make it float.
wetsInto      what this becomes when water touches it, and wetChance is how readily it soaks:
1 means the moment water reaches it, it is wet. Only water wets things, so wet
ground can sit on top of dry ground without soaking into it.
soaks         this liquid wets the ground it touches (water does)
soakConsumeChance  chance the water is used up each time it wets something
life          frames before it decays into decaysInto (0 = lasts forever)
corrodible    whether acid can eat it
corrosion     how readily this eats through what it touches, and corrodeEmits is the gas left
behind in the hole - which is where the toxic fumes off dissolving acid come from
withersPlants what this turns any growing thing it touches into, and witherChance is how often.
Whatever does it is not used up: the fumes kill what they drift through and carry
straight on. It goes by what grows rather than by a list of names, so a new plant
added to this file is covered without anything else changing.
A note on temperatures: heat spreads by averaging with the four neighbours, so a single cell sitting
next to one flame settles at roughly a quarter of the flame temperature. That is why wood ignites at
150 rather than a realistic 300 - it is the temperature a cell can actually reach next to a fire.
